title: The Listening House
premise: Late-night radio host Xanthe Dunmore starts receiving calls from listeners who died the previous week, each one reciting fragments of a night she has spent thirty years refusing to remember. When her childhood imaginary friend, Wren, appears on her porch unchanged, Xanthe is drawn back to the house on Frost Lane where six children once played a game called Listening — and where something answered. The dead callers are not haunting her; they are warning her that what was invited in never left, and it is coming back for the only witness still alive. Holding out until sunrise, Xanthe must finally speak the truth aloud — that she survived by inviting the thing to take the others — and offer herself in exchange before the frost finishes writing its final pattern on the windows.
about_author: Juniper Okonkwo is the pen name of a former overnight radio producer who spent years answering calls from strangers at 3 a.m. and swears half of them were already gone. The Listening House is their second novel, written entirely between midnight and dawn.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. During her 3 a.m. call-in show, a caller describes his own drowning from last Tuesday, then thanks her for 'keeping the door open.' She assumes a prank and cuts him off, but the board lights up with more dead voices. Emotional beat: professional composure cracking into unease.

chapters.title: The Porch
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Arriving home at dawn, she finds Wren — her imaginary friend from age seven — waiting on the porch, unchanged after thirty years. He says only: 'It remembered your voice.' She slams the door and tells herself she hallucinated. Emotional beat: denial as armor.

chapters.title: Second Caller
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The next night, a woman who died in a house fire calls in, speaking in a child's cadence, asking if Xanthe remembers the rules of Listening. Xanthe ends the show early and finds frost on her apartment windows in July. Emotional beat: fear sharpening into recognition.

chapters.title: Frost Lane
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, with a flashback to childhood. She drives to her hometown and stands before the abandoned house on Frost Lane, where six children played Listening in the winter of 1994. Only five graves exist. Flashback shows young Xanthe covering her ears while the others listened. Emotional beat: guilt surfacing.

chapters.title: Wren Explains Nothing
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Wren reappears inside her car, patient and wrong-eyed, insisting he isn't there to scare her but to keep her talking until sunrise — because talking is how you hold the door shut. Emotional beat: reluctant alliance with something impossible.

chapters.title: The Fifth Grave
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. At the cemetery she finds four children's headstones from 1994 and one fresh grave with no name, dated last week. The ground is warm. A fifth caller phones her cell: a man's voice, adult now, saying 'You left me listening.' Emotional beat: dread of being hunted.

chapters.title: What Was Invited
chapters.summary: Alternating past/present. The full childhood game is revealed: the children invited 'the Quiet' to listen through them, and it took them one by one. Young Xanthe survived by offering it a better bargain — someone else, someday. Present-day Xanthe realizes the debt has come due. Emotional beat: horror of complicity.

chapters.title: Sunrise Clause
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Wren explains the rules: the Quiet can only claim her between sunset and sunrise, and only if she stops speaking the truth. If she confesses aloud what she did before the frost completes its pattern on every window, the contract can be rewritten. Emotional beat: fragile hope.

chapters.title: Static
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. She returns to the radio station intending to confess on air, but the station is empty, the equipment playing her own voice from 1994. Every call light is lit. The dead are all trying to warn her off — confession will free the Quiet to take everyone who ever heard her. Emotional beat: trapped.

chapters.title: The Listeners Who Died
chapters.summary: Multi-POV vignettes of the dead callers in their final week, each having dreamed of Frost Lane after hearing Xanthe's show. They weren't random victims; they were collateral, gathered like kindling. Emotional beat: grief for strangers, weight of consequence.

chapters.title: Houseguests
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. She barricades herself in the Frost Lane house at dusk, choosing to face the Quiet on its own ground. Wren sits with her. Frost begins crawling across the windows in patterns that spell names. Emotional beat: grim resolve.

chapters.title: First Window
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The first window fills completely with frost, and the temperature drops. She hears the five dead children listening outside, or wearing the shapes of listening. She talks to them — memories, apologies — and the frost slows. Emotional beat: confession as survival tool.

chapters.title: Wren's Secret
chapters.summary: Wren's POV (strange, childlike). Wren reveals he is not imaginary: he is the fragment of the sixth child, the nameless grave, the one Xanthe bargained away — given shape by her guilt so he could come back and give her a chance to undo it. Emotional beat: devastating tenderness.

chapters.title: The Bargain Revisited
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. She tries to renegotiate: take me instead, spare everyone. The Quiet answers through the frost — it doesn't want her death, it wants her voice, forever, broadcasting its listening to the world. Emotional beat: the price is worse than death.

chapters.title: Interference
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. She realizes the radio was never a coincidence: the Quiet found her through the broadcast tower, and every listener who tuned in became a potential door. She must go dark — permanently — to starve it. Emotional beat: sacrifice of identity.

chapters.title: Third Window
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Three windows frosted, two remain. The dead children press at the glass, and among them she sees her adult self, listening. The Quiet shows her the future: her show continuing, her voice hollowed into its instrument. Emotional beat: temptation and terror intertwined.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. With one window left, she uses a battery-powered transmitter to broadcast her confession to the town: the game, the bargain, the deaths, her guilt. Speaking the whole truth aloud, she feels the frost stop mid-pattern. Emotional beat: catharsis through exposure.

chapters.title: The Final Pattern
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The Quiet, denied her silence, pours itself against the last window. Wren steps outside to meet it, offering himself as the sixth listener at last, completing the circle and closing the contract. The frost melts. Dawn comes. Emotional beat: heartbreak and release.

chapters.title: Aftermath, On Air
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Weeks later, she hosts her final broadcast, announcing retirement, telling her audience a version of the truth most will laugh at. Callers are living again. But one line stays open, silent, breathing. Emotional beat: bittersweet closure.

chapters.title: The Empty Chair
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. She visits the nameless grave, now marked with a stone she paid for: WREN, WHO LISTENED SO OTHERS COULD SPEAK. She reads aloud to it, keeping her promise to never stop telling the truth. Emotional beat: mourning made into ritual.

chapters.title: Someone Else's Show
chapters.summary: New host Marisol's POV. A rookie takes over the 3 a.m. slot at the old station. Her first caller is a child asking if she remembers the rules of Listening. In the window behind her, frost begins to form — in July. Emotional beat: cyclical dread.

chapters.title: Keeping the Door Open
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, epilogue. Living far from any tower, Xanthe receives one last call on an old landline: Wren's voice, thanking her, telling her the door is closed as long as someone keeps telling the truth about what they survived. She leaves the line open and sleeps until sunrise. Emotional beat: hard-won peace.
